**Solution 1 is wrong.** Its argument gives only g(n) = Ω(n^{2/3}), which says nothing about whether g(n)/n tends to 0. In fact g(n)/n is bounded below by a positive constant: the 3-AP hypergraph of a weak Sidon set has at most n edges, so its average degree is at most 3, and standard independent-set bounds for 3-uniform hypergraphs then give an independent set of linear size.

**Solution 3 is wrong.** Its lower bound of 2n/3 rests on an unproven claim that the transversal number is at most n/3. A concrete counterexample is A = {0, 1, 2, 4, 7, 12, 20, 33, 54, 88}. I checked that all sums of distinct pairs are distinct, so A is weak Sidon. Its 3-APs are (0,1,2), (0,2,4), (1,4,7), (2,7,12), (4,12,20), (7,20,33), (12,33,54), (20,54,88). The set {2, 7, 12, 20} meets every one of them, so removing it leaves a Sidon subset of size 6 < 2·10/3. This shows h(A) < 2n/3 here. The same family (a_k = F_{k+1} − 1) has a 3-AP structure whose maximum AP-free density is 3/5, so g(n)/n is at most about 3/5 along this family, which rules out 2/3 as the limit.

**Solution 2 gives 3/5.** Its Fibonacci-type upper bound is consistent with my checks: the maximum AP-free density in that family is 3/5. Its matching lower bound, however, is only asserted (the "careful analysis" is not shown). I also could not rule out that other configurations, such as one resembling the Fano plane, push the limit below 3/5. So I cannot certify 3/5 as the exact answer. It is the only candidate not contradicted by my checks, so I select it as the most plausible, but with real uncertainty.

CHOICE: 2
